preview_text: สี ความชื้น และตำแหน่งของรอยโรคที่ผิวหนังไม่ได้เป็นเพียงรายละเอียดเท่านั้น แต่ยังเป็นตัวชี้ให้เห็นความไม่สมดุลภายในที่ทำให้เกิดโรคอีกด้วย ด้วยการรักษา TCM ที่ถูกต้อง ปัญหาผิวเรื้อรังหลายๆ...
synonyms: ["Cutaneous Lesions", "Skin Blemishes", "Pale Skin Lesions", "Skin lesions that are pale or light-coloured", "Chronic Skin Lesions and Subcutaneous Nodules", "Skin lesions or subcutaneous nodules in chronic cases"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, a skin lesion is any area of skin that looks different from the surrounding tissue. Lesions can be flat or raised, red, brown, or pale, and may itch, weep, or cause pain. They are commonly caused by infections, allergies, autoimmune reactions, or chronic inflammation, and are diagnosed through visual examination, sometimes with a biopsy or allergy testing.
Treatments typically target the visible symptoms with topical steroids, antihistamines, or antibiotics, but the underlying trigger often remains unclear. This can leave patients cycling through creams without lasting relief.
conventional_treatments: Standard care includes topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation, oral antihistamines for itching, and moisturizers to repair the skin barrier. For infections, antibiotic or antifungal creams are used. In more severe cases, oral immunosuppressants or biologic drugs may be prescribed. Phototherapy is another option for certain chronic rashes.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the skin is considered an extension of the internal organs, especially the Blood, Liver, and Spleen. When an organ system is out of balance, it often manifests on the skin. For example, if the Blood is overheated by stress or spicy food, the heat pushes outward and creates bright red, hot, itchy patches. If the Blood is too weak to nourish the skin, it becomes dry, scaly, and easily irritated by external wind.
The Liver and Spleen also play key roles. Dampness and heat trapped in the Liver channel can overflow along its pathway, causing weeping, burning lesions on the groin, chest, or sides. A weak Spleen fails to manage body fluids, so dampness accumulates and seeps into the skin as pale, oozing patches that come and go. When emotional stress blocks the flow of Qi and Blood, the skin may develop dark, purplish, fixed nodules that are painful to touch.
This is why two people with what looks like the same rash might need completely different treatments. TCM doesn't just ask 'what does the lesion look like?' - it asks 'what is the state of your blood, your digestion, and your emotions?' The answer points to the true root of the problem.
tcm_diagnosis:
When lesions appear suddenly as bright red patches, bumps, or hives that feel hot and itch intensely, a practitioner suspects Heat in the Blood. This pattern often flares after wind exposure, spicy food, or emotional stress. The tongue is red with a thin yellow coating, and the pulse feels rapid and sometimes wiry, confirming that heat has entered the blood and stirred up wind on the skin.
If the skin weeps clear or yellow fluid, forms blisters, and feels swollen and burning, Damp-Heat is usually behind it. This pattern often settles along the Liver channel, appearing on the sides of the body, groin, or chest. A bitter taste, irritability, and a greasy yellow tongue coating are strong clues. The pulse is slippery and rapid, showing that dampness and heat are brewing together.
Chronic lesions that are dry, rough, and scaly, with itching that worsens at night, point to Blood Deficiency allowing External Wind to stir. The blood is too thin to nourish the skin, so it becomes parched and easily irritated. The tongue often looks pale and dry, and the pulse is thin. Fatigue, dizziness, or a pale face often accompany this picture, reflecting the deeper lack of blood.
When skin lesions are pale, not very red or hot, and ooze only a little but keep coming back, Spleen Deficiency with Dampness is often at work. The Spleen is too weak to transform fluids, so dampness accumulates. Key signs are poor appetite, bloating, and loose stools. The tongue is pale with a white coating, and the pulse feels soft or slow, confirming that the digestive system needs support to clear the dampness.
Long-standing lesions that turn dark, purplish, or leave stubborn brown marks suggest Qi and Blood Stagnation. Over time, the flow of blood and energy has become blocked, leading to nodules, thickened skin, or fixed pigmentation. The tongue may appear purplish with dark spots, and the pulse feels wiry or choppy. This pattern often follows earlier inflammation and can bring a dull, nagging pain.

patterns.symptoms: ["Bright red skin eruptions", "Intense itching and burning sensation", "Feeling of internal heat, worse at night", "Thirst with desire for cool drinks", "Restlessness and irritability", "Flushed red face"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol and coffee, Stress and anger, Hot showers or saunas, Exposure to wind and heat
patterns.better_with: Cooling foods and drinks, Cool environment, Rest and sleep, Gentle movement
patterns.why_this_happens: When excess Heat enters the Blood, it agitates the blood and pushes it outward to the skin, causing bright red, hot, and intensely itchy eruptions. This Heat often comes from external Wind-Heat invasion or from strong emotions that generate internal Fire. The Heat disrupts the Heart and Liver, leading to restlessness, a flushed face, and a feeling of heat that worsens at night.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with red spots or prickles, thin yellow dry coating. Pulse: rapid (Shu), wiry (Xian), slippery (Hua), and forceful.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Heat in the Blood is a pattern of excess Heat that agitates the blood. Anything that adds Heat-spicy foods, alcohol, emotional stress, hot environments-will flare the condition by further heating the blood. Cooling foods and drinks, rest, and a cool environment help clear Heat and calm the blood, reducing redness and itching.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, alcohol, and coffee. Eat cooling foods like cucumber, watermelon, mung beans, and drink chrysanthemum tea. Keep the skin cool and avoid hot showers or saunas. Gentle exercise like walking or yoga helps circulate Qi without overheating.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Dampness and Heat accumulate in the Liver channel, they can overflow into the skin along the channel's pathway. The Heat makes the lesions red, swollen, and burning, while the Dampness causes oozing, vesicles, and a tendency to weep. This often appears in areas the Liver channel travels, such as the groin, genitals, inner thighs, or lower abdomen, and is commonly seen in conditions like herpes zoster or moist eczema.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Red body with redder sides, yellow greasy coating thicker at the centre and root. Pulse wiry, slippery, and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy, greasy foods and alcohol directly generate Dampness and Heat, pouring fuel on the fire that erupts through the skin. Emotional stress stagnates Liver Qi, which quickly turns into Heat and flares the lesions. A cool, dry environment and a bland diet starve the Damp-Heat of its raw materials, while rest helps the Liver Qi flow smoothly so the skin can calm down.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and sugary foods, as well as alcohol, which all create Dampness and Heat. Eat more cooling, damp-draining foods like mung beans, celery, cucumber, and lightly cooked greens. Manage emotional stress with gentle exercise and relaxation, because bottled-up frustration can fan the Liver Heat. Keep the affected skin clean and dry.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dry, flaky, rough skin", "Itching worse at night", "Pale or sallow complexion", "Aversion to wind or drafts", "Rashes that appear and disappear suddenly", "Dull or brittle nails", "Scanty or pale menstrual blood in women"]
patterns.worse_with: Dry, windy weather, Stress and overwork, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol, Nighttime
patterns.better_with: Rest and sleep, Moisturizing the skin, Warm, not hot, baths, Nourishing, warm foods, Gentle massage
patterns.why_this_happens:
Blood is responsible for nourishing and moistening the skin. When Blood becomes deficient, the skin loses its nourishment and becomes dry, rough, and flaky. This dryness weakens the skin's protective barrier, allowing external Wind to invade easily. The Wind stirs in the skin, causing itching that comes and goes or shifts location, much like a breeze that moves unpredictably.
Because nighttime is yin time and Blood is a yin substance, the itching often worsens at night when Blood fails to anchor the mind and moisten the skin. The overall Blood Deficiency also shows up as a pale complexion, dizziness, and brittle nails.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white and slightly dry coat. Pulse: fine (thin), wiry on the left guan position, and may feel floating at the superficial level.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood deficiency makes the skin dry and vulnerable; dry wind further depletes moisture and stirs itching. Rest and nourishing foods replenish Blood and yin, improving skin moisture. Spicy and fried foods generate heat that consumes Blood, worsening dryness. Wind exposure directly aggravates the external Wind pathogen. Avoiding these triggers and moisturizing helps maintain skin integrity and reduce itching.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat blood-nourishing foods like black sesame, goji berries, dark leafy greens, and bone broth. Avoid spicy, greasy, and overly drying foods that consume Blood. Protect skin from wind and dry air; use a humidifier and gentle, fragrance-free moisturizers. Manage stress and get enough sleep to support Blood production.

patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked meals, Rest and sleep, Gentle movement, Dry, warm environment
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is responsible for transforming food and fluids into usable energy. When it becomes weak, it cannot manage moisture properly, allowing Dampness to accumulate internally. This excess Dampness then overflows into the skin, creating pale, mild lesions that tend to ooze very little but keep coming back. The digestive symptoms like bloating and loose stools are the root of the problem, not just a side effect.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, white greasy coating, moist surface. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slow (Huan), soft and lacking force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen is easily weakened by cold, damp, and overwork. Raw and greasy foods demand extra digestive effort, creating more internal Dampness. Warm, easily digestible meals support the Spleen's transformative function and help drain moisture. Rest and gentle movement restore Qi without depleting it, while emotional strain like worry knots the Spleen Qi, so a calm mind allows the energy to flow smoothly and keep the skin clear.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like congee, soups, and stews. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen. Gentle daily movement like walking helps move Qi and dry Dampness without exhausting you.

patterns.why_this_happens: Emotional stress or frustration blocks the Liver's ability to keep Qi moving smoothly, leading to stuck Qi. Over time, this Qi stagnation causes Blood to congeal and stagnate, obstructing the channels that nourish the skin. The result is dark, purplish, or nodular skin lesions that are fixed in location and may feel stabbing or tender to touch.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots and distended sublingual veins. Pulse: wiry (弦) and choppy (涩), like a taut guitar string scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work:
Stress and anger tense the Liver, further blocking Qi flow and worsening Blood stasis, so calming the mind and moving the body ease the stagnation.

Cold constricts vessels and congeals Blood, while warmth dilates them and encourages flow. Gentle exercise and warm foods help invigorate Qi and Blood, gradually lightening dark, stubborn skin lesions.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, blood-moving foods such as turmeric, ginger, black fungus, and a moderate amount of lean red meat. Avoid cold, raw foods and iced drinks that can congeal Blood. Gentle daily exercise like walking or yoga helps move Qi and Blood. Practice stress-reduction techniques to prevent Liver Qi stagnation from worsening the lesions.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if I've tried every cream without success?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is one of the most common reasons people turn to TCM. Because TCM treats the internal imbalance that produces the skin lesion, it often helps when topical treatments have failed. The approach is fundamentally different - rather than suppressing the rash, we aim to resolve the underlying heat, dampness, or deficiency so the skin can heal from within.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a big role in skin health from a TCM perspective. In general, you'll want to avoid spicy, greasy, and sugary foods that generate heat and dampness. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern - for example, someone with Blood deficiency may need more nourishing, iron-rich foods, while someone with Damp-Heat should cut out dairy and alcohol. Even small changes can make a noticeable difference.

faqs.question: Will acupuncture treat the skin directly?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture needles are sometimes placed near the lesion, but more often we choose points on the body that regulate the affected organ systems - such as the Spleen, Liver, or Blood. The goal is to rebalance the internal environment so the skin clears naturally. Many patients find that acupuncture also reduces stress, which is a common trigger for skin flares.

faqs.question: How long until I see results?
faqs.answer: It varies by pattern. Acute, hot rashes may improve within days to a couple of weeks. Chronic, dry, or weeping lesions take longer because they involve deeper deficiencies - you might see initial improvement in 4-6 weeks, with significant clearing over 3-6 months. Your practitioner will track changes in your tongue, pulse, and lesion appearance to gauge progress.

faqs.question: Can I use my prescribed creams while taking herbs?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. Herbs and acupuncture can be safely combined with topical steroids or moisturizers. However, always tell both your TCM practitioner and your dermatologist about everything you're using. Over time, as your skin improves, you may be able to reduce or stop the creams under medical supervision - but never stop a prescribed medication abruptly without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for children with eczema?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM offers gentle options for children, including mild herbal washes, pediatric acupuncture (with very fine needles or non-needle techniques), and dietary adjustments. The formulas are tailored to the child's size and constitution. Always work with a practitioner experienced in treating children, and inform your pediatrician about any herbs being used.

faqs.question: What if my skin gets worse at first?
faqs.answer: Occasionally, a healing crisis occurs where the skin temporarily flares as toxins are expelled. This is not common but can happen, especially with oozing lesions. Your practitioner will warn you if this is likely and will adjust your formula if the reaction is too strong. Any severe or sudden worsening should be reported immediately - see our Safety section for red-flag symptoms.

research.title: Acupuncture for Chronic Urticaria: A Randomized, Sham-Controlled Trial
research.description: This 2017 randomized controlled trial compared active acupuncture to sham acupuncture in 330 adults with chronic spontaneous urticaria. After 4 weeks of treatment, the active acupuncture group showed significantly greater reductions in itch severity and wheal size compared to sham, with benefits persisting at follow-up. The study provides high-quality evidence for acupuncture as an effective treatment for hives, a common type of skin lesion.
research.periodical: Li Y, et al. Acupuncture for Chronic Urticaria: A Randomized, Sham-Controlled Trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2017;167(10):693-702.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for atopic dermatitis: a systematic review
research.description: This 2013 systematic review evaluated randomized controlled trials of oral Chinese herbal medicine for atopic dermatitis. The meta-analysis found that Chinese herbal medicine significantly improved clinical severity scores and reduced itching compared to placebo, though the quality of many included trials was limited. The review highlights the potential of herbal formulas like Xiao Feng San and Dang Gui Yin Zi for managing eczematous skin lesions.
research.periodical: Tan HY, et al. Chinese herbal medicine for atopic dermatitis: a systematic review. British Journal of Dermatology. 2013;169(4):740-747.
